title: The Heavenly Circuit Practice
author: Mingde
excerpt: The Heavenly Circuit practice makes the true qi circulate through the body in a heavenly circuit, thereby moving the qi, invigorating the blood, dissolving stagnation and stasis, returning the essence to nourish the brain, and thus warding off illness, strengthening immunity, and prolonging life.

inline.s: Appendix: Reverse Abdominal Breathing

The Heavenly Circuit practice makes the true qi circulate through the body in a heavenly circuit, thereby moving the qi, invigorating the blood, dissolving stagnation and stasis, returning the essence to nourish the brain, and thus warding off illness, strengthening immunity, and prolonging life.

Because the breath is the driving force that propels the circulation of the true qi, great attention is paid to breathing in the practice of the Heavenly Circuit. In the course of practice, reverse abdominal breathing — inhaling and exhaling through the nose — is used; for details see the appendix:
Reverse Abdominal Breathing
Practice
“The Five-Step Method of True Qi Circulation”

; once the Ren and Du meridians have been opened, you may practice the Small Heavenly Circuit. Each session of the Small Heavenly Circuit has two major steps: first, gathering the true qi — this is the preliminary stage; then, the heavenly-circuit circulation — this is the main stage. For posture, walking, standing, sitting, or lying are all acceptable, with sitting or standing as the primary forms. The eyes may be open or closed, and the tongue touches the palate. The breath is reverse abdominal breathing — in and out through the nose, fine, even, deep, and long.

[The Ren and Du meridians] The Ren meridian and the Du meridian. The Ren governs all the yin of the body, and the Du governs all the yang. When the “Ren and Du meridians” are opened, qi and blood flow freely. [The Ren meridian] From the Chengjiang point beneath the lower lip, along the very center of the front of the body, down to the Huiyin point directly below the body between the two legs — this channel is the Ren meridian. The Ren meridian governs the six yin channels, runs along the center of the abdomen, and has the function of overseeing and presiding over the qi of all the body’s yin channels, regulating the qi and blood of the yin channels; it is the “sea of the yin meridians.” [The Du meridian] The Du meridian, by contrast, starts from the Huiyin point, travels upward along the spine to the rear, reaches the Baihui point at the crown of the head, then passes forward between the two eyes to the Yinjiao point on the upper palate. The Du meridian governs the six yang channels
, and has the function of commanding and urging on the qi of all the body’s yang channels

; whenever the yang qi is weak, suitable points can be found on the Du meridian for treatment. [Tongue touching the palate] In qigong practice, “the tongue presses the upper palate,” so that the Ren and Du meridians connect — this is called the “Magpie Bridge.”

At this point the preparations are complete, and you may proceed to the next step, the “heavenly-circuit circulation.”

With one inhalation and one exhalation, the true qi sets out from the dantian, travels one full circuit along the Ren and Du meridians, and returns to the dantian, with the intention following the qi (this point — the intention following the qi — is very important; never lead the qi with the intention). On inhalation, contract the perineum, and the true qi passes through the tailbone and ascends along the Du meridian to reach the Baihui point; on exhalation, relax the perineum, and the true qi descends along the Ren meridian into the dantian. Whenever the mouth is full of saliva — this is the most precious golden fluid and jade nectar — swallow it down at once.

When doing walking meditation, inhale every four steps and contract the perineum; exhale every four steps and relax the perineum. The true qi performs its heavenly-circuit circulation in time with the breath.

[Huiyin (perineum)] The Huiyin point is a key point on the Ren meridian of the human body. It is located in the hollow between the anus and the genitals. The Huiyin point and the Baihui point at the crown of the head form a straight line, and are the passageway for the body’s essence, qi, and spirit. The Baihui is yang and receives the qi of heaven, while the Huiyin is yin and gathers the qi of earth; the two depend on each other, correspond to each other, and together govern the normal circulation of the true qi along the Ren and Du meridians, maintaining the balance of yin and yang, qi and blood in the body. It is a vital point of the body’s life activity. Li Shizhen, in his study of the Eight Extraordinary Meridians, discussed it thus: the Huiyin point is the junction of the Ren meridian, the Du meridian, and the Chong meridian, an important point on the Eight Extraordinary Meridians; this point is the source from which vitality springs forth, maintaining the balance of the body’s qi, blood, yin, and yang, and is therefore also a point of longevity. The term “Huiyin point” is the name used in traditional Chinese medicine; the Daoists call it the “Yin Heel,” and in the school of yoga it is called the “root chakra.” Every school and tradition praises the cultivation of this region highly.
Contract the anus slightly, and lift it up within:
inhale, contracting the anus (the grain passage) and secretly lifting the perineum

[To contract (cuō) the grain passage] To contract the anus. As the saying goes: “Contract the anus a hundred times a day, and cure illness, dispel disease, and prolong your years.” The specific method is: on inhalation, use a little force to lift the anus upward together with the perineum; on exhalation, relax them together; repeat ten to twenty times each session, three to five sessions a day being appropriate.
The King of Medicine,

Sun Simiao (miǎo) greatly esteemed this method; in his book Prescriptions from the Pillow he urged the world: “The grain passage should be contracted often.” He held that the muscles around the anus must be kept in intermittent motion to nourish life and strengthen the body, and that it is especially effective in preventing and treating hemorrhoids.
One turn at the tailbone, and on toward the spine-gate:
the true qi in the dantian passes through the perineum, makes one turn at the Weilu (tailbone) gate, and proceeds to the Jiaji (spine) gate.
The Jade Pillow is hard to pass — gaze up toward the crown:
when the true qi
reaches the Yuzhen (Jade Pillow) gate after its long journey, if its strength is insufficient, gaze inward at the crown of the head and use intention to guide the true qi through the Yuzhen gate.

after the true qi passes the Yuzhen gate, it ascends to the crown of the head (Baihui), and following the Du meridian

Down the twelve-storied tower, descend slowly:
the twelve breastbones, each with a rib attached, make twelve pairs of ribs that form the chest cavity

. The “twelve-storied tower” refers to the entire chest cavity. “Down the twelve-storied tower, descend slowly” means that the segment where the true qi follows the exhalation all the way to the dantian (as shown by the green line in the figure above) proceeds slowly. This is because the exhalation route is short while the inhalation route is long, so during exhalation one proceeds slowly, making the exhalation time roughly equal to the inhalation time, or slightly longer.
The divine water of the Jade Pool, swallow it again and again:
the divine water of the Jade Pool is the saliva beneath the tongue in the mouth

, and this is the most precious “golden fluid and jade nectar.” Whenever it brims over, swallow it down at once. The “Jade Pool” is the immortal pool on Mount Kunlun in legend; in the practice, it refers by metaphor to the area under the tongue in the mouth
Straight into the dantian, where the sea’s bottom is void:

the true qi goes straight into the dantian and rests there — that is, “every breath returns to the navel,” as the “Sixteen Ingots of Gold” says. The “sea bottom” is the Huiyin (perineum) point; “the sea’s bottom is void” means that at this moment the perineum is relaxed (the next cycle begins again with an inhalation, contracting the anus and secretly lifting the perineum — “contract the anus slightly, and lift it up within”).

So, in one heavenly-circuit cycle, the true qi begins at the dantian (“contract the anus slightly, and lift it up within”) and ends at the dantian (“straight into the dantian, where the sea’s bottom is void”). The dantian is the sea of qi, the place where the true qi gathers.

Before ending each session, first keep the intention on the dantian for a while, then relax the intention; rub the palms together until warm, rub the face several times as if washing it, then comb the hair with the ten fingers for a while. Once the spirit has returned to normal, slowly rise and move about.
The Sixteen Ingots of Gold” — because this practice is so precious, the ancients likened it to sixteen ingots of gold, meaning that each character is an ingot of gold.
The
Sixteen Ingots of Gold says
With one inhalation, lift at once, and every breath returns to the navel
with one lift, swallow at once, and fire and water meet each other

[With one inhalation, lift at once, and every breath returns to the navel] This means using reverse abdominal breathing to perform the heavenly-circuit circulation. Therefore the heavenly-circuit circulation begins with an inhalation, as the Song of the Heavenly Circuit says. “Lift at once” is what the Song of the Heavenly Circuit calls “contract the anus slightly, and lift it up within” — contracting the perineum. “With one inhalation, lift at once” means that on each inhalation you contract the perineum. “Every breath returns to the navel” means that in every cycle the true qi returns to the dantian, which is what the Song of the Heavenly Circuit calls “(the true qi) goes straight into the dantian.”

[With one lift, swallow at once, and fire and water meet each other] “With one lift, swallow at once” does not mean that you perform the swallowing action with every lift of the anus. Rather, because of “with one inhalation, lift at once, and every breath returns to the navel,” saliva is produced in the mouth — this is what the Song of the Heavenly Circuit calls “the divine water of the Jade Pool, swallow it again and again.” “Fire and water meet each other” means that because the true qi circulates along the Ren and Du meridians in a heavenly circuit, the heart and kidneys interact, and fire and water are in mutual aid.

[Heart-kidney interaction, fire and water in mutual aid] The heart dwells in the chest, belongs to yang, and, among the five phases, is fire; the kidneys are in the abdomen, belong to yin, and, among the five phases, are water. The relationship of mutual dependence and mutual restraint between heart and kidneys is called heart-kidney interaction, also called the mutual aid of fire and water. When this relationship between heart and kidneys is disrupted and becomes pathological, it is called heart-kidney non-interaction. The heart is positioned above and belongs to yang; it governs fire and by nature is active. The kidneys are positioned below and belong to yin; they govern water and by nature are still. The heart-fire must descend to the kidneys and, together with the kidney-yang, warm the kidney-yin so that the kidney-water is not cold. The kidney-water must ascend to aid the heart and, together with the heart-yin, nourish the heart-yang so that the heart-fire does not flare. If the kidneys lacked the fire of the heart, their water would be cold; if the heart lacked the water of the kidneys, its fire would blaze. The heart must be moistened by the kidney-water, and the kidneys must be warmed by the heart-fire. In the normal physiological state, this relationship of fire and water in mutual aid is conditioned importantly upon the dynamic balance of the ascent and descent of heart and kidney yin and yang. Hence it is said: “In the life of a person, the heart is the fire, dwelling above; the kidneys are the water, dwelling below. The water can ascend and the fire can descend; with this one ascent and one descent, never ceasing, life is preserved.” (From the treatise On Ministerial Fire in Further Discourses on the Investigation of Things)

So, the Sixteen Ingots of Gold is in fact an abridged version of the Song of the Heavenly Circuit: with one inhalation and one exhalation, the true qi travels one full circuit along the Ren and Du meridians, the heart and kidneys interact, and fire and water are in mutual aid.

The Great Heavenly Circuit is practiced on the foundation of the Small Heavenly Circuit. Besides the Ren and Du meridians, the route of the true qi’s circulation also runs through other meridians, so that spirit and qi unite closely and embrace without separation, thereby achieving the aim of prolonging life. Because the true qi, besides traveling along the Ren and Du meridians, also flows through other meridians, it is called the Great Heavenly Circuit in contrast to the Small Heavenly Circuit.
Once you are proficient in the Small Heavenly Circuit, you may practice the Great Heavenly Circuit. The method is as follows:
1. Preliminary stage (gathering the true qi): the same as in the Small Heavenly Circuit. If you do this practice immediately after the Small Heavenly Circuit, the preliminary stage may be omitted.
2. Main stage (heavenly-circuit circulation): stand with the feet shoulder-width apart, the hands hanging down, relaxed and still,
the eyes may be open or closed, and the tongue touches the palate. The breath is reverse abdominal breathing — in and out through the nose, fine, even, deep, and long.

Breathe deeply and slowly. On inhalation, contract the perineum, and the true qi ascends along the back of the body into the Baihui point at the crown of the head; on exhalation, relax the perineum, and the true qi descends along the front of the body to the Yongquan points at the soles of the feet. With each breath, the true qi completes one circuit of the Great Heavenly Circuit, with the intention following the qi
(this point — the intention following the qi — is very important; never lead the qi with the intention)
. Whenever the mouth is full of saliva — this is the most precious golden fluid and jade nectar — swallow it down at once.

When doing walking meditation, inhale every four steps, contract the perineum, and think of the Baihui point; exhale every four steps, relax the perineum, and think of the Yongquan point. The true qi performs the Great Heavenly Circuit circulation in time with the breath.

3. Concluding the practice: before ending each session, first keep the intention on the dantian for a while, then relax the intention; rub the palms together until warm, rub the face several times as if washing it, then comb the hair with the ten fingers for a while. Once the spirit has returned to normal, slowly move about freely.

Reverse abdominal breathing is also called dantian breathing. On inhalation, draw in the abdomen and contract the perineum; on exhalation, expand the abdomen and relax the perineum. When first using reverse abdominal breathing, do not strive for fineness, evenness, depth, and length; it is enough just to get the abdomen moving. As your skill deepens, the breath will naturally become deeper and longer, and the number of breaths per minute will grow fewer and fewer, until gradually you achieve fineness, evenness, depth, and length.

At first, the rising and falling of the lower abdomen may be quite pronounced. Once you are proficient, you can reduce the amplitude of the movement, gradually reaching the state of “as if present yet not present, as if absent yet not absent.” At this point the whole body is relaxed, open, and unobstructed.

Reverse abdominal breathing changes the volume of the abdominal cavity during respiration, but its focus is not the air breathed in and out, but the true qi (internal qi). Therefore, reverse abdominal breathing is nominally a way of breathing air, but in essence it is the “breathing” (rising, falling, and surging) of the internal qi. Reverse abdominal breathing is very beneficial to physical and mental health; some people have cured many chronic illnesses merely by practicing reverse abdominal breathing. To dispel illness and prolong life, do reverse abdominal breathing as much as possible in daily life.

If you are not yet accustomed to reverse abdominal breathing, set aside time to practice this breathing method on its own; practice for a few minutes at every opportunity, and the more times a day, the better, until gradually it becomes relaxed and natural and finally forms a habit.

In the early stage of learning, you may silently recite the word “draw” on inhalation and the word “expand” on exhalation, to help you perform the action of “drawing in the abdomen on inhalation and expanding it on exhalation.”
